h1: Fire Damage Restoration in El Mirage, Arizona
intro: The fire is out, the trucks are gone, and you are standing in a house that still smells like it. Maybe the damage looks smaller than you expected and you are wondering if you can just scrub the walls yourself. Maybe it looks worse than you expected and you cannot make yourself walk into the back bedroom yet. Either way, there is a stack of things nobody handed you instructions for: what to throw away, what the adjuster needs, whether the kids can sleep here tonight, why your eyes sting every time you open the door. That is a lot to carry alone, and it is normal to still be carrying it.

sections.eyebrow: What happens in the first days
sections.heading: Why smoke keeps causing damage after the fire is over
sections.body: Fire damage does not stop when the flames do. Soot is acidic, and on a hot Arizona afternoon it keeps eating into whatever it settled on. Within a day or two you can see etching on chrome fixtures and appliance trim. Within a week, uncoated metal starts to corrode, grout and unsealed tile hold the odor, and plasticized surfaces like vinyl window frames and blind slats begin to yellow permanently. Anything porous, drywall, carpet pad, insulation, MDF cabinet boxes, absorbs the smoke residue and keeps releasing odor when the house warms up. The other quiet problem is water. Suppression water soaks into subfloor, bottom plates and wall cavities, and in a closed-up house it does not simply dry off. That is why fire jobs are usually water jobs at the same time, and why the drying side of the work matters as much as the soot cleanup. If your loss involved a lot of suppression water, the process on our water damage restoration page runs alongside the fire work rather than after it. The practical order most fire losses follow: secure the opening and the roof so nothing else gets in, get power and safe access sorted out, document everything before it is disturbed, remove unsalvageable material, clean and deodorize what stays, dry the structure, then rebuild.

sections.heading: What the housing stock here means for a fire loss
sections.body:
El Mirage is really two building eras stacked on top of each other, and they fail differently after a fire.

The original townsite near El Mirage Road and Thunderbird has small postwar and mid-century houses, some of them block, with additions and rewiring done over decades by different hands. In those homes the surprises tend to be inside the walls: old wiring spliced into newer circuits, blown-in or batt insulation that has to come out because it holds odor, and layered ceilings where a popcorn or textured surface sits over an older one. Anything from that era can also mean asbestos-containing texture, floor tile or mastic, which has to be tested and handled properly rather than sanded or scraped in a hurry.

The other El Mirage is the late-1990s-through-2000s tract growth out toward Dysart and Cactus, and along the Loop 303 side. Those houses are wood frame with engineered trusses, OSB sheathing and shared attic space over long roof runs. Smoke travels the attic fast and drops into rooms that never saw flame, so a kitchen fire on one end of the house can leave soot film in a bedroom at the other end. Two-story tract homes also stack the mechanical chase, which gives smoke a straight vertical path.

Seasonally, two patterns show up here. Monsoon storms in July through September bring lightning and hard outflow winds, and they also mean an open roof or a tarped window is an urgent problem, not a next-week problem. Then in the cooler months, the causes shift to space heaters, dryer lint, garage workshops and outdoor fire pits in yards where a June and July stretch above 110 has left everything bone dry. Anything with a west-facing wall or an attached garage in this part of the West Valley tends to run hot, which is hard on wiring and on aging HVAC equipment.

sections.heading: What we do, and who does it
sections.body: Gold Water Fire handles the whole arc of a fire loss so you are not the general contractor of your own house. That means emergency board-up and stabilization, soot and residue cleaning by surface type, HVAC and duct attention so the system stops redistributing odor, structural drying where suppression water went, controlled demolition of what cannot be saved, and then the rebuild. The rebuild is where a lot of homeowners get stranded, because mitigation and reconstruction are often two different companies with two different schedules. Brandon Gurr is our Construction Manager and leads the reconstruction and rebuild side, with Johnny as Reconstruction Team Lead. Framing, drywall, texture match, cabinets, paint and flooring go back in under the same roof as the cleanup. We are licensed in Arizona under AZ ROC #264344, KB-2. You can see the full scope of that work on our reconstruction and rebuild page, and the details of the fire process on our fire damage restoration page. On the paperwork side, Kristine handles office admin and Brooke handles water and mitigation scheduling, so calls and documentation are not falling into a voicemail box. We document conditions and scope as we go, which is what your insurance carrier will ask for. Jim Bennett and Jake Taylor founded the company, and you can read more about the people on it on our about page.

cards.body: Openings covered, roof tarped, structure secured so weather, dust and anyone wandering by stay out while decisions get made.

If you are not sure whether your address is in range, call and ask. It is a short question with a straight answer.

faqs.q: Do I have to move out of my house after a fire?
faqs.a: It depends on how much of the structure and the mechanical systems were affected, whether power and water are safe, and how much smoke residue is in the air handling system. Some losses are one room and the family stays. Others need the house empty while demolition and drying run. We will tell you plainly what we see, and your insurance policy may include loss of use coverage for temporary housing if you cannot stay.

faqs.q: Can I just clean the smoke smell myself?
faqs.a: You can clean hard, nonporous surfaces yourself, and it helps. What household cleaning usually cannot fix is odor stored in porous material: drywall, insulation, carpet pad, cabinet boxes and duct interiors. If the smell comes back strongest when the house heats up in the afternoon or when the AC cycles on, the source is still in the building, not on it.

faqs.q: Will you work with my insurance company?
faqs.a: Yes. We document conditions, scope and materials as we go, in the format carriers ask for, and we communicate with your adjuster through the mitigation and rebuild phases. You still own the claim and the decisions, we just make sure the file is not missing what it needs.

faqs.q: Who handles the rebuild after the cleanup is done?
faqs.a: We do. Reconstruction is led by our Construction Manager, Brandon Gurr, with Johnny as Reconstruction Team Lead, and we hold AZ ROC license #264344, KB-2. You are not handed off to a separate contractor to start the process over from the beginning.
